title: India’s Cockroach Party Protests Have a Powerful Precedent—and It Isn’t the Arab Spring | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Sadanand Dhume argues the global media's framing of India's Cockroach Janta Party Gen-Z protests as an Arab Spring or Nepal/Bangladesh-style regime collapse is vastly overblown; the real analogue is India's own 1974-75 Jayaprakash Narayan movement, driven then and now by youth unemployment, corruption, and an oil-price shock. India's scale, non-political army, and dispersed power centers make street ouster implausible, but Indira Gandhi also looked unassailable until voters removed her twenty-one months after she declared the Emergency.

insights.claim: A 1975 New York Times quotation of Indian opposition leader Jayaprakash Narayan — describing rotten institutions, outdated education, high prices, ubiquitous corruption and rising unemployment — is indistinguishable from the rhetoric of India's 2026 Gen-Z protests, showing the grievances are recurrent rather than novel.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Treating the protests as a cyclical Indian phenomenon rather than a contagion event argues against pricing an imminent regime break into Indian assets.
insights.quote: Everything in the country is rotten. The system of education is outdated. The students don’t see a ray of hope.

insights.claim: Media comparisons of India's Cockroach Janta Party protests to the 2011 Arab Spring or to the recent government collapses in Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are vastly overblown, and the better comparison is India's own 1974-75 student movement.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The consensus narrative of imminent South Asian contagion is the trade to fade; headline risk is being over-extrapolated from smaller states.

insights.claim: The political parallels to mid-1970s India are structural: a long-serving prime minister who vanquished intra-party rivals and diminished the opposition, accusations of a cult of personality, eroded democratic institutions, a media brought to heel, and ruling-party supporters who spot foreign plots everywhere.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging whether Indian political risk is following the 1970s template — institutional erosion plus youth joblessness was the pre-Emergency signature.
insights.quote: Then, too, critics accused the prime minister of cultivating a cult of personality, eroding democratic institutions, and bringing the media to heel.
insights.locator: The parallels with India in the mid-1970s are striking

insights.claim: The 1973 OPEC oil shock damaged India's energy-import-dependent economy in the same way the ongoing war in Iran is damaging it now, making an external energy price shock a shared precondition of both protest waves.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Direct macro linkage: Indian domestic political stability is levered to crude, so an Iran-driven oil spike is also an Indian political-risk input.
insights.quote: The 1973 OPEC oil shock hurt India’s energy import dependent economy much like the war in Iran is doing now.
insights.locator: The external environment also shared similarities

insights.claim: India's 1974-75 protest movement ended with Indira Gandhi suspending democracy and declaring an Emergency in June 1975, and when she called elections twenty-one months later voters removed her from office in a turning point of Indian political history.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The historical template resolves at the ballot box on a roughly two-year lag, not in the streets — the relevant date to watch is the next national election, not the next march.
insights.quote: India’s protest movement of 1974–1975 eventually led to Indira Gandhi suspending democracy and declaring an “Emergency” in June 1975.

insights.claim: Narendra Modi is deeply aware of the 1970s precedent because his home state of Gujarat was the birthplace of the 1974 protests and he cut his political teeth as a Hindu nationalist activist opposing Indira Gandhi's Emergency.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Modi's personal history with this precedent makes rapid concession rather than escalation the likelier government playbook, capping tail risk of a 1975-style crackdown.

themes.theme: Youth jobs shock and the AI threat to Indian IT

insights.claim: About 30 percent of India's 1.5 billion people are between fifteen and twenty-nine, making job scarcity a mass rather than marginal political problem.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The demographic dividend is also the political risk base: roughly 450 million people in the cohort most exposed to labour-market failure.
insights.quote: About 30 percent of India’s 1.5 billion people are between fifteen and twenty-nine.
insights.locator: The CJP has tapped into a deep vein of discontent

insights.claim: A study by economists at Azim Premji University found that 40 percent of Indian graduates under the age of twenty-five are unemployed, and many of their families took on debt to pay for that education.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Debt-financed education with a 40 percent graduate unemployment rate is a household balance-sheet problem as much as a political one — watch Indian consumer credit quality.
insights.quote: A recent study by economists at Azim Premji University found that a staggering 40 percent of Indian graduates under the age of twenty-five are unemployed.
insights.locator: And concerns about jobs loom large among the young

insights.claim: Artificial intelligence threatens India's large information technology sector, which has ceased to be a reliable source of middle-class jobs.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: AI disruption of Indian IT services is now being cited as a driver of street politics, not just an earnings story — a second-order political cost for the sector's outsourcing model.
insights.quote: Artificial intelligence threatens India’s large information technology sector, which has ceased to be a reliable fount of middle-class jobs.
insights.locator: Artificial intelligence threatens India’s large information technology sector

insights.claim: In May the Indian government voided the NEET national medical examination taken by more than two million aspiring doctors after evidence emerged the questions had leaked in advance — the second time in three years the exam was compromised.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: A repeat failure affecting two million families is the specific trigger that converted diffuse economic anxiety into organized protest.
insights.quote: In May, the government voided a national medical examination taken by more than two million aspiring doctors after evidence emerged that the questions had leaked in advance.
insights.locator: A broken examination system has compounded these anxieties

insights.claim: A 2024 Indian Express investigation counted forty-one major exam leaks across fifteen states over five years, with criminal cartels — some linked to India's massive test-prep industry — turning the procurement and sale of exam papers into a business.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Systemic, not one-off, credentialing failure implicates the listed Indian education and test-prep complex in the political backlash.
insights.quote: A 2024 investigation by the Indian Express counted forty-one major exam leaks spanning fifteen states over the previous five years.

themes.theme: How the Cockroach Janta Party scaled and forced concessions

insights.claim: The Cockroach Janta Party took its name from a May remark by India's chief justice likening unemployed youth to 'cockroaches', was founded by Abhijeet Dipke — a thirty-year-old public-relations master's graduate then living in Boston who called on X for 'all cockroaches' to come together — and within weeks its Instagram following dwarfed that of the ruling BJP.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: A diaspora-founded, platform-native movement out-scaled the ruling party's social reach in weeks — evidence that incumbent digital dominance in India is not defensible.
insights.quote: Within weeks the CJP’s following on Instagram dwarfed the BJP’s.
insights.locator: The Cockroach Janta Party gets its name

insights.claim: Activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protests in late June and began a June 28 hunger strike demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan; as his health declined the government appeared to panic and police forcibly moved him to a government hospital on July 18.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The government's handling of a single high-profile activist was the escalation point — a template for how symbolic figures amplify diffuse protest movements.
insights.quote: As the fifty-nine-year-old activist’s health declined, the government appeared to panic.
insights.locator: On June 28, Wangchuk began a hunger strike

insights.claim: A July 20 attempt by thousands of protestors to march on India's Parliament House was blocked by police and paramilitaries using batons, tear gas and pellet guns, injuring at least sixty protestors and more than one hundred police by police count (the CJP claims about one hundred and fifty protestors injured), and viral footage forced the prime minister into a late-night Instagram video before Education Minister Pradhan resigned on July 25.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The government conceded a cabinet resignation within five days of a viral crackdown — the demonstrated response function is rapid appeasement, which lowers escalation risk but invites further demands.
insights.quote: Videos of police brutality quickly flooded social media, forcing the prime minister to record a late-night Instagram video three days later to defuse the situation.
insights.locator: Two days later, thousands of protestors attempted to walk to Parliament House

themes.theme: Why India will not break like its smaller neighbors

insights.claim: India is structurally resistant to street-driven regime collapse because the government retains a firm grip on the bureaucracy, police and paramilitaries, the Indian army — unlike peers in many developing countries — has never meddled in politics, and the country's sheer size makes it impossible to paralyze by flooding the national capital.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The base case for Indian assets is disruption without discontinuity — protest headlines should not be traded as coup or collapse risk.
insights.quote: The sheer size of the country makes it impossible to paralyze simply by flooding the national capital.
insights.locator: The Indian government retains a firm grip

insights.claim: Unlike Bangladesh, Egypt, Libya, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Tunisia, India's political, financial and technological power is not concentrated in a single city — the same dispersion that protects the United States from capital-city capture.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: Geographic dispersion of power centers is a transferable screen for judging which countries' protest movements can actually topple a government.
insights.quote: political, financial, and technological power in India are not concentrated in a single city
insights.locator: Like the United States, and unlike Bangladesh

insights.claim: Modi is unlikely to meet the fate of Egypt's Hosni Mubarak or Bangladesh's Sheikh Hasina, but Indira Gandhi also looked unassailable right up until the moment Indians got to vote again, so he should brace for stormy days ahead.
insights.speaker: Sadanand Dhume
insights.so_what: The risk to Indian policy continuity is electoral and multi-year, not immediate — position for gradual political drift rather than an abrupt change of government.
insights.quote: Indira Gandhi also looked unassailable, right up until the moment Indians got to vote again.
